name: Johann Sebastian Bach
note: Independent lines that form a larger architecture.
listen: Follow a short figure as another voice takes it up; keep listening to the bass when the upper part becomes busy.

name: George Frideric Handel
note: Opera, oratorio and keyboard music across languages and borders.
listen: Listen for a melody that could be sung, then notice how rhythm and harmony give the phrase direction.

name: Antonio Vivaldi
note: Ritornello, contrast and the energy of the concerto.
listen: Notice the recurring orchestral material between the soloist’s episodes. Each return helps you find your place.

name: Arcangelo Corelli
note: The trio sonata and concerto grosso as models of balance.
listen: Hear the two upper parts trade phrases above a moving bass; in the concertos, compare the small and larger groups.

name: Claudio Monteverdi
note: A turning point between Renaissance polyphony and Baroque drama.
listen: Hear how a change in the words can alter the pace, harmony or number of voices.

name: Henry Purcell
note: English theatre, song and the expressive force of a ground bass.
listen: Follow a repeating bass and listen to how the melody changes its meaning above it.

name: Georg Philipp Telemann
note: An unusually wide musical world: chamber music, church and opera.
listen: Listen for changes in instrumental colour and the different dance characters within a suite.

name: Domenico Scarlatti
note: Keyboard sonatas full of crossings, leaps and unexpected turns.
listen: Hear repeated notes, sudden changes of register and exchanges between the hands within a compact keyboard sonata.

name: Alessandro Scarlatti
note: Cantata and opera in the Neapolitan tradition.
listen: Compare a speech-like recitative with the more settled pace and returning material of an aria.

name: François Couperin
note: Character pieces, ornament and the meeting of French and Italian tastes.
listen: Listen for ornaments within the melodic line and the contrasting characters of successive keyboard pieces.

name: Louis Couperin
note: Unmeasured preludes and the freedom of a musical gesture.
listen: In an unmeasured prelude, follow the harmony and gestures without expecting a regular dance beat.

name: Jean-Philippe Rameau
note: Harmony as both a theoretical subject and a theatrical force.
listen: Notice how a repeated dance figure changes through harmony, register and ornament.

work.title: Nouvelles suites de pièces de clavecin

name: Jean-Baptiste Lully
note: Dance, court spectacle and French musical tragedy.
listen: Compare the dotted rhythms of an overture’s opening with the quicker imitative passage that follows.

name: Dieterich Buxtehude
note: Organ improvisation, sacred music and the Abendmusiken.
listen: Follow the bass pattern in a passacaglia; in a prelude, hear the shifts between free passages and imitation.

name: Johann Pachelbel
note: Chorale variation and a much wider keyboard world beyond the Canon.
listen: Keep the repeating bass in mind while the upper voices enter at different times.

name: Girolamo Frescobaldi
note: Toccatas that turn time and keyboard touch into an expressive art.
listen: Listen to changes of pace and figuration as a keyboard gesture leads into another.

name: Heinrich Schütz
note: The German sacred tradition shaped through encounters with Venice.
listen: Follow the text through overlapping vocal entries and contrasts between small and larger groups.

name: Johann Jakob Froberger
note: Keyboard suites, travel and a meeting of European styles.
listen: Compare the freedom of a toccata with the rhythmic character of a suite’s dances.

name: Johann Joseph Fux
note: Court music and a lasting language for teaching counterpoint.
listen: Listen to the independence of the vocal lines and to the ways one part answers another.

name: Heinrich Ignaz Franz Biber
note: Violin writing, resonance and scordatura.
listen: Listen for chords and multiple lines within a violin part; some sonatas require altered string tuning.

name: Marin Marais
note: The viola da gamba as an intimate, speaking instrument.
listen: Hear the bass viol move between melody, ornament and chordal writing.

name: Marc-Antoine Charpentier
note: Sacred and dramatic music between French and Italian traditions.
listen: Notice the contrast between solo voices and ensemble, and how dissonance gives weight to a word.

name: Élisabeth Jacquet de La Guerre
note: Harpsichord suites, sonatas and opera from a composer at the French court.
listen: Follow the dance pulse beneath the harpsichord ornaments; compare it with the dialogue of the sonatas.

name: Barbara Strozzi
note: Cantatas and song built around the expressive possibilities of a solo voice.
listen: Follow the singer’s declamation and the bass beneath it; expressive words often receive harmonic emphasis.

name: Francesca Caccini
note: Song, court performance and early opera at the Medici court.
listen: Listen for speech-shaped melody and the exchanges between solo singing and ensemble.

name: Isabella Leonarda
note: Sacred vocal music and instrumental sonatas from convent life.
listen: Hear how short melodic ideas pass between instruments and how sections change pace.

name: Jan Dismas Zelenka
note: Sacred counterpoint with striking rhythmic and harmonic turns.
listen: Follow an active bass against the upper lines; listen for unexpected harmonic turns.

name: Francesco Geminiani
note: Italian violin writing and the concerto grosso abroad.
listen: Compare the solo group with the larger ensemble and hear the ornaments within the melodic line.

name: Carlos Seixas
note: Portuguese keyboard sonatas at the edge of Baroque and galant styles.
listen: Listen for the rhythmic character of the keyboard figures and the contrast between their registers.

name: Juan Cabanilles
note: A Spanish organ tradition of tientos and contrapuntal invention.
listen: Follow the imitative entries of a tiento, then compare the repeated patterns of a pasacalles.

name: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach
note: Expressive pauses, sudden changes and the intimate sound of the clavichord.

name: Wilhelm Friedemann Bach
note: Learned counterpoint beside unusually free fantasias and dances.

name: Johann Christian Bach
note: The London Bach: a younger generation’s clear melody and lighter textures.

name: Johann Christoph Friedrich Bach
note: The Bückeburg Bach: keyboard miniatures alongside court music and larger vocal works.
